heroLede: This report studies more than 100 open-source projects in the Agentic AI ecosystem and compares them with established software repositories. It looks at how agents are entering everyday development work, and what open infrastructure must manage when their actions reach production. Final abstract to be confirmed.
voicesIntro: Opening notes on the Agentic AI ecosystem.
zhengyuQuote: Quote to be confirmed before publication.
xuQuote: Quote to be confirmed before publication.
mergeGateBody: Agents already read repository rules, edit code and run tests. The contribution surface now includes machine-readable instructions and plugins alongside issues and pull requests.
executionGateBody: An agent can generate code during a task, call an external tool and carry state across several short-lived environments. The process may disappear in minutes; its effects do not.
landscapeOverviewTitle: Agent applications lead the activity. Runtime is where the landscape is filling in.
landscapeOverviewBody: The current landscapes contain 84 Agent Infra and 59 Model Infra projects. Applications hold 55% of Agent Infra's July OpenRank, while Runtime accounts for 13 of the 23 Agent Infra selections outside the May tracking pool. Model Infra remains an older, Python-led systems base, with Serving holding 44% of its July OpenRank. The findings below follow recent growth, project age, primary language and the runtime path from context to evidence.
landscapeTitle: Applications hold the activity. Runtime holds more of the new selections.
agentChartTitle: Attention is still concentrated at the application layer
modelChartTitle: Serving still carries the systems weight
ageFinding: The agent layer is being invented quickly. Most of the infrastructure underneath it predates the current wave and is being asked to carry a different task shape.
languageTitle: Agent products lean TypeScript. Model infrastructure still speaks Python.
languageBody: TypeScript leads Agent Infra with 33 of 84 repositories; Python leads Model Infra with 33 of 59. The split reflects two engineering centres: product-facing agent tools and a model stack rooted in ML and systems work.
runtimePathTitle: Runtime projects are clustering along the path an agent takes through a task.
runtimePathBody: The map is filling in around context, interfaces, tool execution, isolation and evidence. Coding agents create the demand; these runtime categories show what the rest of the stack has to provide.
growthSummary: Recent OpenRank gains appear around tool use, context and inference efficiency. They show community activity, not production adoption.
outsideGithubTitle: Usage data also points toward coding agents and open-weight models.
outsideGithubBody: GitHub remains the main record of how projects are built. Public usage and model-hub data provide a narrower outside check: whether an application is being called and whether model artifacts are being reused.
collaborationTitle: Agents are already part of the workflow. They rarely start the thread.
collaborationLede: We followed 2,000 Issues and pull requests from 100 repositories in the Top 100. The public record shows where Agents appear, what they do, and where a GitHub User or maintainer still has to make the call.
collaborationAdoptionTitle: Repository rules moved first. Visible Agent participation followed.
collaborationAdoptionBody: Machine-readable Agent instructions now appear in 86 of the Top 100 repositories. In the probability sample, verified Agent identities or App-mediated User actions appear in 89 of 100 repositories. The two measures describe readiness and observed participation; neither tells us how much code was written with AI.
collaborationTasksTitle: The visible work is concentrated in review, triage and response.
collaborationTasksBody: Verified Agent identities produced far more public review, routing and discussion events than thread openings or attributed commits. These are observable GitHub events, not a census of AI-written code: local assistance and private maintainer work leave no reliable public trace.
collaborationEntryTitle: Agents gather in the middle of the thread.
collaborationEntryBody: Agent participation opens less than one percent of sampled threads, yet appears in about a third of PR review. Agents are far more visible after submission than at the point where an Issue or PR enters the project.
collaborationIterationTitle: Review still produces a real revision loop.
collaborationIterationBody: A visible review appears in six out of ten sampled PRs. More than half of reviewed PRs add another commit, and nearly three quarters do so after a change request. The trace shows iteration; it does not tell us whether the reviewer caused the change or whether an Agent saved maintainer time.
collaborationGovernanceTitle: Open contribution remains the norm. More projects ask contributors to align before coding.
collaborationGovernanceBody: All 100 repositories enable Pull Requests, but creation access is not identical. Ninety-eight allow anyone to create one; Codex and Claude Code restrict creation to collaborators. Twelve more use an Issue-first or scoped pre-approval rule. DeepSeek Harness remains a useful outlier outside the denominator: public code, closed core contribution and a plugin-led extension path.
collaborationBurdenTitle: More automated review does not settle the efficiency question.
collaborationBurdenBody: Agent-visible threads contain more comments and reviews, and their resolved PRs carry the GitHub merged flag more often. Agent participation is selected, however, and can arrive because a change is important or difficult. The association is real; the productivity claim is not identified.
collaborationScarcityTitle: The scarce contribution is a decision that survives review.
collaborationScarcityBody: External accounts create most pull requests in the weighted sample. Their resolved PRs carry GitHub's merged flag far less often than maintainer or member submissions. Code is abundant at the entrance; review, task selection and a defensible gate remain scarce.
caseTitle: The contribution surface sits outside the core repository
caseQuote: “You may consider this repository an idea, an official showcase, and a source of inspiration, but not a mandate from us.”
caseBody: The project treats its official code as a reference point and third-party plugins as the place where the ecosystem can branch out. That arrangement leaves practical governance work around interface stability, discovery and what happens when a plugin becomes unsafe or abandoned.
governanceInterface: Interface stability needs a visible owner.
governanceDiscovery: Plugin discovery needs verification and provenance.
governanceRevocation: Unsafe or abandoned capabilities need a revocation path.
studyNote: The thread estimates use a frozen Top 100, a 2,000-thread repository-stratified probability sample and an equal-repository view. GitHub User means account type, not human-written code. GitHub merged flag is not a universal accepted-contribution label.
infrastructureTitle: The runtime can disappear while its authority and effects remain.
infrastructureLede: Kubernetes and OpenStack already carry production AI workloads. Agents introduce a task that can create code, borrow authority and leave effects in several systems. The figures below describe the installed base, not Agent adoption.
closingQuestion: Can an agent run code, use authority and leave enough evidence for someone else to understand what happened?
closingNote: This is where agentic AI meets cloud native, PyTorch and OpenInfra. The established stack remains useful. Its control model has to account for code and environments that appear during the task.
